analysis.one_liner: Bans the commercial sale, resale, or rental of cribs that don't meet federal and industry safety standards.
analysis.headline: The Infant Crib Safety Act drew 37 bipartisan backers but never received a hearing or a vote, dying in a House subcommittee at the end of the 106th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill made it illegal for manufacturers, resellers, rental companies, child care providers, and hotels to make, sell, lease, or provide a crib that fails federal safety regulations and ASTM industry standards. It was aimed especially at unsafe secondhand, hand-me-down, and heirloom cribs, which the bill's findings say cause most crib deaths. Violators faced fines up to $1,000, and anyone could sue to stop sales of unsafe cribs.
analysis.who_benefits: Infants and their families: the bill targeted the roughly 9,000 children under age 5 injured in cribs each year and the at least 45 who die from crib injuries annually, concentrated in older secondhand cribs. Families would gain assurance that any crib bought, rented, or provided by a day care or hotel met safety standards.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for any commercial user — manufacturers, resellers, leasing companies, child care facilities — to manufacture, sell, or lease a crib that is unsafe for any infant.
Bars hotels, motels, and similar lodging from providing unsafe cribs to guests.

Presumes a crib unsafe unless it meets federal crib regulations (16 CFR parts 1508, 1509, 1303) and ASTM voluntary standards F966, F1169, and F1822, closing the gap on older secondhand cribs that existing law did not cover.

Backed by findings that more than 9,000 children age 4 and under are treated in hospitals for crib injuries each year, at least 45 die, and most crib deaths involve secondhand, hand-me-down, or heirloom cribs.

analysis.who_pays: Crib resellers, thrift and consignment shops, rental companies, hotels, and child care providers would bear the cost of screening, repairing, or retiring non-conforming cribs. Families who rely on cheap secondhand cribs could face fewer available hand-me-downs or higher costs for a compliant crib. Manufacturers would need to certify products against a long list of standards.

drawbacks.text: Because as many as 2 out of 4 infants are placed in secondhand or heirloom cribs while only about 1 million new cribs are sold for nearly 4 million births each year, restricting resale of non-conforming cribs could leave some low-income families with fewer affordable options, a cost the bill's own findings imply.

Enforcement is modest: the fine for knowing violations is capped at $1,000, so compliance would depend heavily on private injunction lawsuits, which carry attorneys' fees and could press hard on small thrift stores and family child care homes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and concrete — fewer infant deaths and injuries in the old cribs that cause most of them. The costs fall on sellers and lodging and child care businesses that would have to verify crib standards, and on families who depend on the secondhand market, since the bill restricted resale without funding a replacement program for low-income households. The small fine and reliance on private lawsuits make enforcement thin, but the core safety mandate is straightforward.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection subcommittee, where it sat — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — until the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Ellen Tauscher (D-CA) introduced the Infant Crib Safety Act on July 12, 1999, with 19 original cosponsors from both parties.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the day it was introduced.
On July 21, 1999, it was sent to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection, where no further action was taken.
The bill gathered 36 cosponsors, 33 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but never received a committee vote or floor action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that sold, leased, or provided non-conforming secondhand cribs — resale shops, rental companies, hotels, and child care providers — avoided new compliance costs, and no infant deaths were prevented by a law that never passed.

for.name: Rep. Ellen Tauscher
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Infant Crib Safety Act and recruited a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: 36 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, including original cosponsors Rep. Greenwood (R-PA) and Rep. Barrett (D-WI) from the Commerce Committee's home turf.

against.name: House Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee that controlled the bill's fate
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two remaining years of the Congress.

against.name: Resale, lodging, and child care businesses
against.role: Businesses that would have had to retire non-conforming cribs
against.what_they_did: Would have borne the compliance cost of screening or retiring used cribs; no organized support for the bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was heavily Democratic — 33 of 36 cosponsors — but the bill had Republican cosponsors too, and its death in a Republican-run committee was procedural inaction rather than a recorded party vote.

industries.industry: Secondhand crib resellers, consignment and thrift shops, and rental companies
industries.note: The bill made it unlawful to resell, lease, or place in commerce any used crib that fails federal and ASTM standards — the core of the bill, since most crib deaths occur in secondhand cribs. Their interest in continuing to sell old cribs ran directly against infant safety.

Lodging facilities would have been barred from offering unsafe cribs to guests, forcing them to maintain compliant loaner cribs or offer none. The cost of compliance falls on the businesses; the benefit is safety for traveling families.

industries.industry: Child care facilities and family child care homes
industries.note: Expressly named as commercial users, they would have had to replace non-conforming cribs, a real expense for small family child care providers. Parents leave infants unattended in these cribs for hours, so the safety gain is direct.

Manufacturers already meet the federal and ASTM standards the bill adopts; restricting the market for non-conforming secondhand cribs would push families toward new, compliant cribs. Their commercial interest and child safety point the same way here.
